m: Departing from what is normal or accepted.
t: Same root as aberration: wandering (errer) off the path. Identical to « aberrant ».

m: Difficult to understand; obscure.
e: Latin abstrusus (hidden), from abstrudere: abs- (away) + trudere (to push). Pushed away out of sight.
t: Same as « abstrus »: an idea pushed so far away you can’t reach it.

m: Sharp and forthright, especially in criticism.
t: « Un ton acerbe ». Same acer as aigre and vinaigre.

m: Refusing to change one’s mind; unshakable.
e: Greek adamas, “unconquerable”: a- (not) + daman (to tame). A legendary unbreakable stone, later diamond.
t: Adamas = the unbreakable stone that gave « diamant ». An adamant person is diamond-hard.

m: Giving or conveying a warning or reprimand.
e: Latin admonere, “to remind, warn”: ad- + monere (to warn), as in monitor.
t: Ad + monere: a monitor warning you. Une admonestation = a reprimand.

m: Of doubtful authenticity, though widely repeated.
e: Greek apokryphos (hidden): apo + kryptein (to hide). The Apocrypha were biblical books excluded as of uncertain origin.
t: Same as « apocryphe ». Like the famous quote nobody actually said.

m: Done openly and unashamedly; very obvious.
e: Coined by Edmund Spenser in The Faerie Queene (1596) for the “Blatant Beast”, a noisy monster of slander; perhaps from Latin blatire (to babble).
t: Spenser’s loud Blatant Beast: blatant things shout at you. « Un mensonge flagrant ».

m: Acting in a confused or clumsy way.
e: From bumble, an imitative English word (like the buzz of a bumblebee), meaning to blunder or ramble.
t: A bumblebee bumping into windows. Inspector Clouseau is a bumbling detective.

m: To grow or increase rapidly; flourish.
t: Burgeon = « bourgeonner »: buds bursting out in spring. A burgeoning start-up scene.

m: To confuse; or to prove wrong.
e: Old French confondre, from Latin confundere, “to pour together”: com- + fundere (to pour).
t: Same as « confondre »: everything poured together. Results that confound the experts prove them wrong.

m: To interpret a meaning.
e: Latin construere, “to pile together, build”: com- + struere (to build). In grammar, to build up a sentence’s meaning.
t: You construct a meaning. Misconstrue = to build the wrong one.

m: Dependent on something uncertain. (n.: a group within a larger one.)
t: The offer is contingent on due diligence: it touches on it and depends on it. « Les contingences ».

m: Abundant, plentiful.
t: « Un repas copieux ». Copia = abundance.

m: Behaviour in keeping with good taste and propriety.
e: Latin decorum (that which is proper), from decere (to be fitting).
t: Identical to « le décorum ». Same family as decorous.

m: To criticise unfairly; belittle.
t: Same as « dénigrer »: blackening someone’s name.

m: Separate and distinct.
e: Latin discretus (separated), from discernere: dis- (apart) + cernere (to sift). Same origin as discreet, split in spelling later.
t: Discrete = distinct units, like discrete maths. Discreet (ee) = « discret », tactful.

m: To destroy completely; wipe out.
e: Latin eradicare, “to pull up by the roots”: e- (out) + radix (root).
t: Radix = racine: pulling the weed out by its root. Same as « éradiquer ».

m: To adopt or support a cause or belief.
e: Old French espouser (to marry), from Latin sponsare, from spondere (to promise).
t: Exactly « épouser une cause »: you marry the idea.

m: Making great demands; strict.
e: From exact (to demand), Latin exigere, “to drive out, demand”: ex- + agere.
t: Exacting = « exigeant », from the same exigere. An exacting partner.

m: To praise highly; raise in rank.
t: Ex + altus = lift up high. « Exalter ».

m: To clear from blame.
t: Onus = burden: lifting the burden of guilt off someone. « Exonérer » in French is mostly about taxes, but same image.

m: To explain in detail.
e: Old French espondre, from Latin exponere, “to put forth”: ex- + ponere (to place).
t: Expound = « exposer » (same exponere). Expounding a theory at length.

m: Willing to share information; also about to happen.
t: Coming forth with information. An unforthcoming witness says nothing.

m: Overused, unoriginal; trite.
e: From hackney, a horse for hire (perhaps from Hackney, the London village). A horse used by everyone became anything worn out.
t: Picture a tired hired horse ridden by everyone. A hackneyed phrase has been ridden to death.

m: Attacking cherished beliefs or institutions.
t: The adjective of iconoclast: smashing sacred images, or sacred ideas.

m: A peculiar habit or way of behaving.
t: Idios = one’s own (as in idiom): your own personal mix of quirks.

m: Dishonourable; base.
t: Not noble. Same as « ignoble ».

m: Unable to be appeased; relentless.
t: Same as « implacable »: impossible to placate.

m: Not seeming reasonable or likely.
t: An excuse nobody would applaud. « Pas plausible ».

m: Not able to be corrected or reformed.
t: Identical to « incorrigible »: beyond correction.

m: Lack of interest or concern. (Also mediocrity.)
e: Latin indifferentia: in- + differre (to differ). It makes no difference to you.
t: Same as « indifférence ». Careful: indifferent can also mean mediocre on the GRE.

m: To bring oneself into favour, often by flattery.
f: s’attirer les bonnes grâces de, s’insinuer
t: Getting into someone’s good graces (gratia). « S’attirer les bonnes grâces ».

m: Unwilling to compromise.
e: Spanish intransigente, from Latin in- + transigere (to come to an agreement).
t: Same as « intransigeant »: no transaction possible.

m: Generosity in giving gifts or money.
t: Identical to « largesse ». A lord throwing coins from his carriage.

m: Deserving praise.
t: Laud = louer (to praise). Laudable = louable.

m: Short-sighted; lacking foresight.
e: Greek myōps, “short-sighted”: myein (to shut) + ōps (eye). Squinting with half-closed eyes.
t: Same as « myope ». A myopic strategy only sees this quarter.

m: Not transparent; hard to understand.
t: Same as « opaque »: light can’t get through, and neither can meaning.

m: Designed to impress; showy.
t: « Ostentatoire »: stretching it out for everyone to see.

m: Overly concerned with minor details and rules.
e: Italian pedante (schoolmaster), probably related to Greek paideuein (to teach).
t: Same as « pédant »: the schoolmaster correcting your commas.

m: Childishly sulky or bad-tempered.
t: Careful: French « pétulant » means lively. English petulant = a sulking toddler.

m: Dealing with things practically, not theoretically.
t: Pragma = action. Same as « pragmatique ».

m: Unsophisticated, narrow-minded.
t: Like parochial: thinking from far away from the capital. « Un esprit provincial ».

m: An expert who gives opinions publicly.
t: A pandit was a learned Hindu scholar. Today’s pundits are TV experts.

m: To restore friendly relations; make compatible.
t: Same as « réconcilier ». You also reconcile two sets of numbers in a model.

m: To prove wrong.
t: Same as « réfuter ». Not just deny: prove false.

m: Causing sleep; very boring.
t: Identical to « soporifique ». A soporific lecture.

m: Moderation, self-restraint (especially with alcohol).
e: Latin temperantia (moderation), from temperare (to mix in due proportion).
t: One of the four cardinal virtues: « la tempérance ». Tempered = mixed in the right dose.

m: Full of twists and turns; overly complex.
t: Same as « tortueux ». Not torturous (painful) — tortuous twists.

m: To emphasise.
e: English under + score (a line, from Old Norse skor, notch). Literally to underline.
t: Underline = « souligner ». The data underscores the risk.

m: Having no moral principles; not honest.
e: un- + scrupulous, from Latin scrupulus (a small sharp stone): the pebble in your sandal that bothers your conscience.
t: Scrupulus = a little stone in your shoe. The unscrupulous feel no pebble at all. « Sans scrupules ».
